# Database Storage and Transaction Internals: Technical Brief

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging
*(from storage-engine-researcher child — covering ARIES, LSNs, checkpointing, group commit, physiological logging, CLRs, and the Postgres/InnoDB WAL split, cross-referenced with LSM and B+Tree maintenance below)*

## 2. MVCC
*(from concurrency-control-researcher child — covering snapshot isolation via xmin/xmax, version chains, VACUUM/purge GC, SSI per Cahill et al., and OCC per Kung & Robinson)*

## 3. LSM Trees
*(from storage-engine-researcher child — covering memtables, SSTables, leveled vs size-tiered compaction, bloom filters, tombstones, write amplification, RocksDB/Cassandra/LevelDB)*

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance
*(from storage-engine-researcher child — covering node splits/merges, Lehman-Yao B-link trees, latch crabbing, copy-on-write B+trees as in LMDB)*

## 5. Two-Phase Commit
*(from concurrency-control-researcher child — covering prepare/commit phases, in-doubt transactions, presumed-abort/presumed-commit, XA heuristics, Spanner's 2PC-over-Paxos)*

## 6. Logical Clocks
*(from distributed-systems-researcher child — covering Lamport timestamps, vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks in CockroachDB, Spanner TrueTime)*

## 7. Quorum Systems
*(from distributed-systems-researcher child — covering Dynamo W+R>N quorums, sloppy quorums/hinted handoff, Paxos/Raft majority quorums, quorum leases)*

## 8. Crash Recovery

Crash recovery is the process by which a database restores a consistent, durable state after an unplanned failure (process crash, power loss, OS crash) using only the persisted write-ahead log and data files. The canonical reference algorithm is **ARIES** (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al., 1992), which structures recovery into three sequential passes over the log: **Analysis**, **Redo**, and **Undo**.

**Analysis phase.** Starting from the most recent checkpoint's `begin_checkpoint` record, ARIES scans forward through the log to reconstruct two in-memory structures that were lost on crash: the **Transaction Table** (listing transactions active at crash time, each with its last LSN) and the **Dirty Page Table** (DPT), which lists pages that were modified in the buffer pool but not yet flushed to disk, each tagged with its **recLSN** — the LSN of the log record that first dirtied the page. This phase determines the **redo point**: the minimum recLSN across all dirty pages, which is the earliest point in the log from which redo work could be required.

**Redo phase.** ARIES redoes the log starting at the redo point, and critically, it **repeats history**: it reapplies every logged update since that point, regardless of whether the owning transaction later committed or aborted, including updates that were already undone. This "redo everything" principle avoids the complexity of distinguishing committed from uncommitted work during this pass. Idempotency is enforced through **LSN stamping**: each data page stores the LSN of the last log record applied to it (**pageLSN**). Before reapplying a logged change, the recovery process compares the log record's LSN to the page's current pageLSN; if the page's LSN is already greater than or equal to the log record's LSN, the update was already persisted and is skipped. This makes redo safe to run even if a crash occurs mid-recovery and recovery itself must be restarted.

**Undo phase.** After redo completes, the Transaction Table identifies **loser transactions** — those active (neither committed nor aborted) at crash time. ARIES undoes their updates in reverse LSN order. Each undo action generates a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**, which records the undo itself and includes a `nextUndoLSN` pointer to the next record requiring undo for that transaction. CLRs are never themselves undone; this guarantees that recovery is restartable and terminates even if the system crashes repeatedly during undo, since the undo work strictly shrinks (each crash-restart skips already-compensated updates by following CLR pointers).

**Checkpointing** bounds the cost of the Analysis phase by limiting how far back in the log recovery must scan. ARIES uses **fuzzy checkpoints**: a `begin_checkpoint` record is written, then the current Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table are flushed asynchronously (without blocking transaction processing or forcing all dirty pages to disk), followed by an `end_checkpoint` record. Because checkpointing doesn't force dirty pages out, it is cheap and frequent, unlike a **consistent checkpoint**, which would require quiescing activity and flushing the entire buffer pool.

**Buffer management policy** determines what recovery must handle. ARIES assumes **steal, no-force**: the buffer manager may *steal* frames from uncommitted transactions (writing dirty pages for active transactions to disk under memory pressure, necessitating undo/CLRs), and need not *force* (flush) all a transaction's pages at commit (necessitating redo). This combination maximizes buffer manager flexibility and throughput at the cost of requiring both redo and undo logic in recovery, as opposed to simpler but less performant **no-steal, force** policies that avoid needing a redo or undo pass respectively.

**Torn-page / partial-write protection.** Physical pages are typically larger than the atomic write unit guaranteed by storage hardware (e.g., a 4KB sector vs. an 8–16KB database page), so a crash mid-write can leave a page **torn** — part old, part new. PostgreSQL addresses this with **full_page_writes**: the first modification to a page after a checkpoint logs the entire page image to WAL, so recovery can restore a known-good full image before replaying subsequent incremental redo records. InnoDB uses the **doublewrite buffer**: before writing pages to their actual data file locations, InnoDB first writes them sequentially to a contiguous doublewrite area; if a crash produces a torn page in the real location, InnoDB detects the corruption (via checksum mismatch) and restores the page from the intact doublewrite copy before applying redo logs.

**LSM-based crash recovery** differs structurally but relies on the same WAL principle. Systems like RocksDB and Cassandra append every write to a WAL before inserting it into the in-memory memtable. On crash, since the memtable is lost, recovery replays the WAL records sequentially to rebuild the memtable's contents before the engine resumes serving reads/writes; because SSTables on disk are immutable and were only ever written after being durably flushed, they require no repair, and WAL segments corresponding to already-flushed SSTables can be safely discarded (tracked via per-SSTable sequence number watermarks).

---

# Storage Engine Internals: WAL, LSM Trees, and B+Tree Maintenance

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging

The governing invariant of WAL is that a log record describing a change must reach stable storage before the corresponding data page is allowed to be written back, and the record must be durable before the transaction that produced it is acknowledged as committed. This underlies the **ARIES** recovery algorithm (Mohan et al., IBM), which structures crash recovery into three passes. The **analysis phase** scans the log from the last checkpoint forward to reconstruct the dirty page table and the list of transactions active at crash time, determining the point from which redo must begin. The **redo phase** replays all logged updates from that point forward, including updates belonging to transactions that will ultimately be undone — ARIES redoes history unconditionally using the page's **LSN** compared against the log record's LSN, skipping work only when the page's LSN already dominates the record's LSN (idempotence via the page-LSN comparison). The **undo phase** then rolls back the losers (transactions uncommitted at crash time) in reverse chronological order using the log's backward chain.

**Log sequence numbers (LSNs)** are monotonically increasing identifiers stamped on every log record and mirrored into the header of each data page that the record modified. This page-LSN is the mechanism that makes redo idempotent and lets recovery determine, without re-executing logic, whether a given page already reflects a given update. LSNs also drive the dirty page table entries used in checkpointing.

**Checkpointing** bounds the amount of log that must be scanned on recovery. ARIES uses **fuzzy checkpoints**: the checkpoint record captures the transaction table and dirty page table *without* flushing all dirty pages to disk synchronously, which avoids the I/O stall of a **consistent (sharp) checkpoint** that quiesces the system and flushes everything before resuming activity. Fuzzy checkpoints trade a slightly more complex analysis phase (since some referenced dirty pages may not yet be on disk) for near-zero disruption to foreground transactions.

The **force-at-commit** rule (the actual "write-ahead" durability guarantee) mandates that a transaction's commit log record be flushed to stable storage before the commit is reported to the client, while the modified data pages themselves may remain in the buffer pool and be written back later (steal/no-force policies in the classic ARIES taxonomy: steal allows uncommitted pages to be written early, no-force allows committed pages to stay dirty). To amortize the fsync cost of force-at-commit, systems use **group commit** (log batching): multiple transactions' commit records are coalesced into a single sequential log flush, trading a small amount of added commit latency for drastically higher commit throughput under concurrency.

ARIES logging is **physiological**: a log record is physical in that it targets a specific page, but logical in that the operation recorded (e.g., "insert this slot into this page") is replayed via the page's own operation logic rather than a raw byte-diff, which keeps log records compact and tolerant of internal page reorganization. This sits between pure **physical logging** (byte-level before/after images) and pure **logical logging** (operation-level, e.g., "increment counter X"), the latter being faster to write but far harder to make idempotent and correctly undoable, since logical undo requires the inverse operation to be well-defined independent of concurrent physical layout changes.

Undo safety under repeated crashes is handled by **compensation log records (CLRs)**. When ARIES undoes an operation during the undo phase, it writes a CLR describing the compensating action and pointing to the next record to undo (via the `UndoNextLSN` field), which means CLRs themselves are never undone — this guarantees recovery terminates even if the system crashes repeatedly during undo.

Concrete real systems diverge in log record structure but follow the same principles. **PostgreSQL's WAL** is physiological, storing full-page images periodically (controlled by `full_page_writes`) to guard against torn pages, with a single unified WAL stream feeding both crash recovery and streaming replication. **InnoDB** (MySQL) separates concerns into a **redo log** (physiological, circular, fixed-size, used purely for crash recovery of committed/in-flight changes to pages) and a separate **undo log** (stored in undo segments, logically structured as old row versions) used both for transaction rollback and for MVCC consistent reads — a redo/undo separation that Postgres does not make at the physical log level since Postgres implements MVCC via heap tuple versions rather than undo-log-based version chains.

## 2. LSM Trees

The **memtable** is the in-memory write buffer, typically a skip list (as in RocksDB and LevelDB) chosen for its lock-free-friendly concurrent insertion and O(log n) ordered access without the rebalancing overhead of a red-black tree. Writes land here first, concurrently appended to a **WAL** for crash safety, since the memtable's contents are lost on crash and must be reconstructed by replaying the log.

When a memtable fills, it is flushed immutably to disk as an **SSTable** (Sorted String Table) — a sorted, immutable, block-structured file with an index and typically a footer containing metadata. Immutability is central to the LSM design: it eliminates in-place update complexity and enables simple, sequential I/O on flush, at the cost of needing a separate reconciliation process (compaction) since logically overwritten or deleted keys now exist in multiple SSTables simultaneously. Deletions are represented by **tombstones** — markers rather than physical removal — which must propagate through reads (a tombstone masks older versions during merge-reads) and are only physically dropped once compaction guarantees no older version of that key survives beneath it, including across all levels that could still be queried.

**Compaction strategy** is the primary tuning lever. **Size-tiered compaction** (Cassandra's default, HBase) groups SSTables of similar size and merges them into one larger SSTable once enough accumulate, trading higher space amplification (multiple overlapping versions can coexist for a while) for lower write amplification. **Leveled compaction** (LevelDB, and RocksDB's `kCompactionStyleLevel`) organizes SSTables into levels of exponentially increasing size with non-overlapping key ranges within a level; a file is compacted into the next level when that level exceeds its size threshold, giving much better read and space amplification at the cost of higher write amplification since a key may be rewritten once per level. RocksDB additionally offers a **tiered+leveled hybrid** (its "leveled" mode already blends ideas, and `kCompactionStyleUniversal` is its size-tiered variant) and lets operators choose per workload, exposing explicit **compaction scheduling** controls — background thread pools, rate limiting, and priority between flush and compaction jobs — to bound write stalls.

**Bloom filters** attached per-SSTable (or per-block, as in RocksDB) let point lookups skip SSTables that provably do not contain a key, which is critical because an LSM read may otherwise have to probe every level. This directly attacks **read amplification**, the cost of checking multiple SSTables per logical read, which is the LSM's structural tradeoff against **write amplification** (the multiplicative rewriting of data across compaction levels) — tuning compaction style is fundamentally about choosing a point on this read/write/space amplification triangle. LevelDB and RocksDB (itself a fork/descendant of LevelDB developed at Facebook) and Cassandra all instantiate these mechanisms concretely, differing mainly in default compaction strategy and in whether the memtable is a skip list (RocksDB, LevelDB) or a different sorted structure.

## 3. B+Tree Maintenance

Standard maintenance operations are **node splitting** on insert, when a leaf or internal node exceeds its capacity, promoting a separator key to the parent, and **node merging** (or redistribution) on delete, when a node falls below a minimum **fill factor** (occupancy threshold), typically 50% in classic B-trees, to bound tree height and avoid pathological sparsity. Implementations often favor lazy deletion or deferred merging over strict minimum-occupancy enforcement, since eager rebalancing increases write amplification on skewed delete patterns.

Concurrent access to a B+tree while splits are in-flight is handled by two complementary mechanisms. **Latch coupling (crabbing)** has a traverser hold a latch on the parent node only until it has acquired a latch on the child, then releases the parent — ensuring no lock is held longer than necessary while preventing a reader from following a pointer into a node being concurrently restructured. The **Lehman-Yao algorithm** underlies **B-link trees**, which add a **right-link pointer** at every node to its right sibling at the same level; this lets a reader that encounters a node mid-split (before the parent has been updated with the new separator) simply follow the right-link to find the newly created sibling node, making the tree safely traversable during splits without requiring the splitting writer to hold locks across the parent update. This decouples split propagation from reader blocking and is the basis of most production concurrent B+tree implementations' latch protocols.

**Copy-on-write B+trees**, exemplified by **LMDB**, avoid in-place page mutation entirely: any update copies the affected leaf and propagates copied pages up to a new root, leaving the old tree structure intact and readable — this gives lock-free, wait-free readers (each transaction simply reads from a snapshot root) at the cost of extra page copying per write and reliance on a single-writer model with MVCC-style root swapping rather than fine-grained latching. **Bulk loading** builds a B+tree bottom-up from pre-sorted data, packing leaves to a target fill factor and constructing internal levels directly, avoiding the incremental split cascade of one-record-at-a-time insertion and yielding much better initial space utilization.

**Page-level versioning for MVCC-compatible B+trees** appears in systems like PostgreSQL's index access methods, where index entries point to heap TIDs and visibility is resolved against the heap rather than stored in the index page itself, and in SQLite's rollback-journal/WAL-mode pager, which can keep multiple page versions referenced by different in-flight readers via its WAL-mode shared cache, conceptually paralleling LMDB's copy-on-write snapshot isolation but implemented at the page-cache level rather than through full structural copy-on-write.

messages.content: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering two areas of database transaction internals: (1) MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control), (2) Two-Phase Commit.

response.content:
# MVCC and Two-Phase Commit: Technical Deep-Dive

## 1. Multi-Version Concurrency Control

**Snapshot isolation via XIDs and tuple visibility.** MVCC's defining mechanism is that writers never block readers and vice versa, because each write creates a new physical or logical version of a row tagged with the transaction identifier (XID) that created it. PostgreSQL implements this directly in the heap tuple header with `xmin` (the XID that inserted/created the version) and `xmax` (the XID that deleted/superseded it, or 0 if live). A transaction running at snapshot isolation acquires a snapshot at (roughly) the start of the statement or transaction, consisting of the set of XIDs considered in-progress at that moment plus a watermark (`xmax` of the snapshot, i.e., the next XID to be assigned). Visibility checks then walk candidate tuple versions and apply rules such as: a tuple is visible if `xmin` committed before the snapshot was taken and either `xmax` is unset or `xmax`'s transaction has not committed (or committed after the snapshot). This yields each transaction a consistent "read view" of the database as of a fixed point in time, without shared locks on read paths. Postgres additionally consults the commit log (`pg_xact`/CLOG) to resolve whether a given XID actually committed, aborted, or is still in-progress, since the raw XID alone doesn't encode outcome.

**Divergent multi-version storage architectures.** A second mechanism worth distinguishing is *where* old versions live. Postgres uses in-place multi-version tuples: every UPDATE produces a brand-new tuple in the same heap, linked to the old one via a forward pointer (`ctid` chain), leaving old versions interspersed with live ones until vacuumed. InnoDB instead keeps the primary record as the single latest version and reconstructs older versions on demand by applying undo log records (stored in the rollback segment) against the current row — essentially an undo-log-based version chain, where each row carries a hidden `DB_ROLL_PTR` pointing to its most recent undo record, which in turn points further back. This is cheaper on the primary data path (no heap bloat from updates) but makes long-running snapshot reads more expensive, since reconstructing an old version requires replaying undo records.

**Garbage collection of dead versions.** Because old versions accumulate, both systems need reclamation mechanisms. Postgres's VACUUM (and autovacuum) scans heap pages for dead tuples — those whose `xmax` committed before the oldest snapshot still active anywhere in the system (the "oldest xmin horizon") — and marks their space reusable, also updating the visibility map and freezing old XIDs to avoid 32-bit XID wraparound. InnoDB's purge threads instead walk the history list of the rollback segment, discarding undo log entries for transactions below the engine's low-water mark (no active read view can still require them), which both reclaims undo space and allows delete-marked rows to be physically removed.

**Write skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation is not truly serializable: it permits write skew, the classic example being two transactions each reading an overlapping constraint (e.g., on-call doctors) and independently writing disjoint rows based on a stale read, violating an invariant no individual transaction's write set would. Cahill, Röhm, and Fekete's SSI (as published in SIGMOD/TODS, "Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases") addresses this by tracking rw-antidependencies — edges where a transaction T1 reads a version that T2 later overwrites — on top of an existing SI implementation, using precision locking (SIREAD locks) to record which transactions read which (possibly not-yet-existing) data rather than full predicate locks. When the antidependency graph forms a specific pattern (two rw-antidependency edges forming a cycle with particular timing), SSI aborts one of the transactions to prevent a serialization anomaly. PostgreSQL implements this as its `SERIALIZABLE` isolation level, layering SIREAD lock tracking and dangerous-structure detection on top of its existing snapshot-based storage engine.

**Validation-based and timestamp-ordering variants.** Not all MVCC implementations are purely multi-version-storage-plus-locking; some use optimistic concurrency control (OCC) in the Kung & Robinson (1981) sense, where transactions execute against a private workspace or snapshot and, at commit, undergo a validation phase checking for conflicting reads/writes against concurrently committed transactions, aborting on conflict rather than blocking during execution. Microsoft's Hekaton (SQL Server's in-memory OLTP engine) combines MVCC with exactly this optimistic validation: transactions read a consistent snapshot via begin/end timestamps embedded in row versions, proceed without locking, and at commit undergo a validation phase (checking the read set for revalidation and the scan set against phantom inserts) before the commit timestamp is finalized — a timestamp-ordering protocol fused with OCC-style validation rather than two-phase locking.

## 2. Two-Phase Commit

**Coordinator/participant roles and the two phases.** 2PC solves atomic commitment across multiple resource managers participating in one distributed transaction. One node acts as coordinator (transaction manager); others are participants (resource managers). In the prepare (voting) phase, the coordinator sends PREPARE to all participants; each participant makes its updates durable (typically via write-ahead log records) but does not yet release locks or make results visible, replying VOTE-COMMIT or VOTE-ABORT. If all vote commit, the coordinator writes a COMMIT log record and enters the commit phase, broadcasting COMMIT; otherwise it broadcasts ABORT. Participants acknowledge and release resources.

**Write-ahead logging and recoverability.** The protocol's durability guarantees rest on WAL: the coordinator writes a PREPARE record (listing participants) before sending prepare messages, and a COMMIT/ABORT record before sending the corresponding decision, ensuring that after a crash the coordinator can replay its log to determine and re-announce the outcome. Participants similarly log their own prepared state before voting, so a recovering participant can rejoin and learn the final decision rather than unilaterally deciding.

**The in-doubt transaction / blocking problem.** If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted commit but before the COMMIT decision is broadcast, those participants are "in-doubt": they hold resources locked, cannot unilaterally commit or abort (either could be wrong), and must block until the coordinator recovers or an operator intervenes. This is 2PC's fundamental fault-tolerance weakness — it is blocking under coordinator failure, which motivated non-blocking alternatives like Skeen's 3PC (adding an extra pre-commit phase so participants can safely decide among themselves) and consensus-based commit protocols such as Paxos Commit (Gray & Lamport), which replicate the coordinator's decision via a Paxos group so no single coordinator failure causes blocking.

**Presumed-abort and presumed-commit optimizations.** To reduce logging and message overhead, practical implementations adopt presumed-abort (if a participant has no record of a transaction, it assumes ABORT, letting the coordinator skip ABORT acknowledgment logging) or, less commonly, presumed-commit. Presumed-abort is the common default (used in the XA standard's typical implementations) since aborts are more frequent and ambiguous unlogged outcomes default safely.

**XA standard and heuristic decisions.** The X/Open XA standard defines the interface between transaction managers and resource managers (databases, message queues) for distributed 2PC, with `xa_prepare`, `xa_commit`, `xa_rollback` calls. When an in-doubt transaction blocks too long, administrators can force a heuristic decision (heuristic commit/abort/mix), after which the transaction is heuristically completed — a manual override that risks violating atomicity and must be reconciled later.

**Relation to consensus-based systems.** Google Spanner combines 2PC across shards with Paxos within each shard: each Paxos group (replicated shard) acts as one participant in a cross-shard 2PC, with the Paxos leader of the coordinator shard playing the coordinator role. This hybrid uses Paxos to make each participant highly available (surviving replica failure) while still relying on 2PC's blocking semantics for cross-shard atomicity, trading away full non-blocking guarantees for practical simplicity at Google's scale.

messages.content: Write a rigorous technical deep-dive covering two areas of distributed database internals: (1) Logical Clocks, (2) Quorum Systems.

response.content:
# Logical Clocks

**Lamport timestamps.** Leslie Lamport's 1978 mechanism assigns each process a monotonically increasing counter. On any local event the counter increments; on message send, the timestamp is attached; on receive, the local counter is set to max(local, received) + 1. This produces a partial order consistent with the **happens-before relation** (→): if a → b, then C(a) < C(b), though the converse need not hold — two concurrent events can still receive comparable timestamps, a false-causality artifact. Lamport clocks totally order events (with tie-breaking by process ID) but cannot distinguish genuine causality from coincidental ordering, which is why they're insufficient for conflict detection in replicated systems.

**Vector clocks.** To capture causality precisely, vector clocks (Fidge, Mattern) maintain a vector of counters, one per process. Each process increments only its own component on local events and merges vectors (component-wise max) on message receipt. Two events are causally ordered iff one vector dominates the other in every component; otherwise they're **concurrent**, denoted a || b. This precise detection of concurrency is exactly what Amazon's **Dynamo** uses to detect conflicting writes across replicas: when a GET returns multiple versions whose vector clocks are incomparable, Dynamo surfaces all of them to the application for semantic reconciliation rather than silently picking one. Cassandra originally used a similar approach before moving toward timestamp-based last-write-wins.

A key distinction: **version vectors** are a restricted application of the vector clock idea to per-replica object versioning in storage systems — one counter per *replica* rather than per *process/thread* — used specifically to detect divergence and enable reconciliation (e.g., in Dynamo, Riak, and the original Ladin/Liskov/Shrira replicated-file-system work). Vector clocks track causality between arbitrary events; version vectors track causality between *object versions* across a fixed replica set. The practical problem with both is unbounded growth: the vector's size scales with the number of distinct replicas/actors that have touched the object, motivating pruning heuristics and bounded vector-clock variants.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** Kulkarni et al.'s HLC combines a physical-time component (synchronized via NTP) with a logical counter, producing timestamps that are close to wall-clock time yet preserve the Lamport happens-before guarantee. Each node tracks `(pt, l)` where `pt` approximates physical time; on events, the node takes max of its physical clock and the previous HLC physical component, incrementing the logical counter `l` only when physical time hasn't advanced or has gone backward relative to causally related events. This gives HLC timestamps that are comparable across nodes without requiring tight clock synchronization, and lets applications treat them like regular timestamps (e.g., for TTL expiry or human-readable ordering). **CockroachDB** uses HLC for its MVCC timestamp ordering and to detect/handle clock skew during transaction commit (uncertainty intervals trigger read refreshes). **MongoDB** uses HLC-derived logical clocks for its causal consistency sessions and to generate cluster-wide `clusterTime`.

**TrueTime (Spanner).** Google Spanner takes a fundamentally different approach: rather than logical counters, it exposes **TrueTime**, an API (`TT.now()`, `TT.after()`, `TT.before()`) backed by GPS and atomic clocks in each datacenter, returning not a single timestamp but a bounded interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain the true time, with bounded uncertainty ε (historically ~1-7ms). Spanner's **commit-wait** mechanism holds a transaction's commit until the TrueTime interval's lower bound exceeds the commit timestamp, guaranteeing external consistency (linearizability) across the globally distributed system without exchanging messages to establish ordering — the physical uncertainty bound substitutes for logical coordination.

**Interval Tree Clocks (ITC).** Almeida, Baquero, and Fonte's ITC generalizes vector clocks for systems with dynamic membership, where the fixed-size vector-per-replica model breaks down as nodes join/leave (e.g., mobile or peer-to-peer systems). ITC represents causal history as a pair of binary trees — an *id* tree (ownership/forking of identity) and an *event* tree (causal history) — supporting `fork` (splitting an id to spawn a new replica without pre-provisioning a slot) and `join` (merging ids back, reclaiming space). This avoids the vector clock's requirement of a known, fixed replica set.

**Causal consistency systems.** **COPS** (Clusters of Order-Preserving Servers, Lloyd et al.) implements causal consistency across datacenters by tracking explicit per-key dependencies: clients attach the causal context (set of dependent key-versions) to writes, and COPS servers check dependencies are satisfied before making a write visible, giving ALPS (availability, low latency, partition tolerance, scalability) properties with causal+ consistency. **Bolt-on causal consistency** (Bailis et al.) takes an orthogonal approach, adding a causal consistency shim layer on top of eventually consistent stores (like Cassandra) without modifying the underlying store, tracking dependencies via metadata and enforcing causal visibility at the client/middleware layer.

# Quorum Systems

**Dynamo-style quorums (W+R>N).** Amazon Dynamo's quorum model parameterizes replication by N (replica count), W (write quorum), and R (read quorum). Writes succeed when acknowledged by W replicas; reads query R replicas and reconcile results. The core correctness rule is **W + R > N**, guaranteeing read and write quorums intersect in at least one replica, so a read overlaps with the most recent write and can detect it (though not necessarily serve only the latest value without further reconciliation via vector clocks). Common configurations like N=3, W=2, R=2 trade off latency, durability, and consistency. Cassandra adopted this same tunable quorum model (ONE, QUORUM, ALL consistency levels per operation).

**Read repair and hinted handoff.** These are quorum-consistency-maintenance mechanisms layered on top of the W/R model. **Read repair** detects, during a quorum read, that some replicas returned stale data and asynchronously (or synchronously) pushes the latest version to those replicas, converging the system toward consistency without a separate repair process. **Hinted handoff** addresses the case where a target replica is unreachable at write time: a different node temporarily accepts and stores the write intended for the unavailable replica (a "hint"), later forwarding it once the target recovers. Together they let Dynamo/Cassandra maintain the sloppy-quorum availability guarantee while still converging replicas.

**Sloppy quorums vs. strict quorums.** A strict quorum requires W or R acknowledgments from the *specific* N replicas designated as an object's natural replica set (by consistent hashing). A **sloppy quorum**, used by Dynamo, instead accepts acknowledgments from any W/R reachable nodes among the "first N healthy nodes" encountered while walking the ring, trading strict replica-set consistency for availability during partitions or node failures — directly embodying the AP side of the **CAP theorem** (sacrificing strict consistency for availability under partition). Strict quorums (as in quorum-based consensus protocols) prioritize consistency, refusing to proceed if a majority/specific quorum is unreachable.

**Paxos quorums.** Classic (single-decree) **Paxos** requires **majority quorums** (⌊N/2⌋+1) in two phases: **Phase 1 (prepare/promise)**, where a proposer sends a prepare request with proposal number n to a majority of acceptors, who promise not to accept proposals numbered less than n and return any previously accepted value; and **Phase 2 (accept/accepted)**, where the proposer sends an accept request with a value (either its own or the highest-numbered previously accepted value returned in phase 1) to a majority, and the value is chosen once a majority acknowledges acceptance. Because any two majority quorums over the same set must intersect, this guarantees safety (no two different values chosen) even under concurrent proposers and node failures, at the cost of the protocol being able to stall (liveness is not guaranteed under the FLP impossibility result without extra assumptions like leader election/failure detectors).

**Raft quorums.** **Raft** (Ongaro and Ousterhout) simplifies Paxos's model with a strong leader and uses majority quorums for two purposes: **leader election**, where a candidate must receive votes from a majority of servers (with the randomized election timeout and term numbers preventing split-vote livelock), and **log replication**, where a log entry is considered committed once the leader has replicated it to a majority of followers, at which point the leader applies it and advances the commit index. The majority-overlap property again ensures that any newly elected leader's log already contains all previously committed entries (via the election restriction that a candidate must have an up-to-date log to win votes).

**Flexible and weighted quorums.** Beyond uniform majorities, **grid quorum systems** arrange replicas in a logical two-dimensional matrix where read quorums take one element from every column and write quorums take an entire row (or similar constructions), reducing the quorum size needed for one operation type at the cost of the other, improving load distribution over strict majority schemes. **Crumbling walls** (Naor and Wool) generalize this by partitioning replicas into groups ("walls") of varying height; a quorum consists of one full wall plus one element from each remaining wall, offering a tunable family of quorum systems with different load and availability characteristics. **Weighted voting quorums** (Gifford's original quorum consensus) assign votes to replicas based on reliability or network proximity rather than treating all replicas identically, letting designers tune fault tolerance asymmetrically.

**CAP tradeoffs and quorum leases.** Quorum systems are a direct mechanism for navigating the **CAP theorem**: strict majority quorums (Paxos/Raft) favor consistency and partition tolerance (CP) at the cost of availability during a loss of majority; sloppy quorums (Dynamo) favor availability and partition tolerance (AP) at the cost of strong consistency, relying on eventual convergence via read repair and conflict resolution. **Quorum leases** (Moraru et al.) optimize the common case where a subset of replicas serves most reads: a replica or replica set is granted a time-bounded lease guaranteeing no conflicting quorum write will occur during the lease period, allowing that replica to serve linearizable reads *locally* without a quorum round-trip, significantly reducing read latency for workloads with geographic locality while preserving the same consistency guarantees as full quorum reads.
